$comment: The substitution graph (JJ-004, JJ-005, JJ-006): what a household may pour when a recipe asks
for something it does not have. This is the file that decides whether 'no Cointreau' ends the
search or offers the Curaçao on the shelf, so it is hand-written and deliberately conservative.
Global only: both ends are shared catalog ingredients. A household's own ingredient satisfies a
recipe line by exact match and never through this graph (JJ-005, JJ-018).
Two shapes, because substitution is not always mutual.
interchangeable - every member stands in for every other, both ways.
oneWay          - 'recipeAsksFor' may be poured as 'youMayPour', and NOT the reverse. A recipe
asking for brandy is happy with cognac; one asking for cognac is not happy
with any brandy, and a graph that pretended otherwise would recommend drinks
the household cannot actually make well.
Both shapes expand to DIRECTED rows (JJ-006): an interchangeable group of three becomes six.
The bar for inclusion is 'a bartender would pour this without comment', not 'these are both
brown'. Bourbon for rye, yes. Mezcal for tequila, no - it changes the drink, and someone who
wants that can fork the recipe.

interchangeable.note: Orange liqueurs. Genuinely swapped behind every bar; the sweetness differs, the drink survives.
Dry gins. Plymouth is softer and London dry sharper, but no recipe breaks on the swap.
American whiskeys. Rye is drier and bourbon sweeter; a Manhattan works with either, and the books disagree about which it wanted.
Aged rums. The line between gold, dark and aged is a marketing decision as often as a production one.
Anise spirits. Absinthe, pastis and anisette differ in strength and sugar, and all three do the job when a recipe wants a rinse or a dash.
Sparkling wines. A recipe topping a drink with bubbles does not care whose.
Bitter aperitivi. Aperol is lighter and sweeter than Campari and the drink shifts, but it is the standard swap and every bar makes it.
Chartreuse. Yellow is milder and sweeter than green; recipes name one and accept the other.
Citrus juice. The Savoy itself writes 'Lemon or Lime Juice' on ten lines, which settles it.
Plain sweetening syrups. Gomme is simple syrup with gum arabic; demerara is darker. Interchangeable by the spoonful.
Ginger. The ale is sweeter and milder than the beer, and a Mule made with either is still a Mule.
Quinquina aperitif wines. All four are bitter, wine-based and hard to find; whichever one a household has is the one it will use.

oneWay.note: Every cognac is a brandy. The reverse is not true, and a recipe naming cognac names it for a reason.
Thin, but the older books use 'brandy' loosely and an apple brandy carries most of them.
A gold rum in a daiquiri is a darker daiquiri, not a mistake. A white rum where the recipe wanted an aged one is a thinner drink, so this does not run the other way.
Both are unaged cane spirits. Cachaça is grassier, so a caipirinha is not improved by white rum and the reverse is not offered.
As cachaça: cane juice rather than molasses, one direction only.
Dissolved sugar is sugar, and syrup saves the stirring. Not the reverse: a recipe calling for syrup is usually shaken, where a sugar cube will not dissolve.
The same thing under two names in two books.
Blanc is sweeter. It carries a martini; a recipe built on blanc's sweetness is not carried by dry.
Thinner and it shows, but the drink is recognisably itself. Never the reverse.
A dash of the wrong bitters beats no bitters at all, and every bar has Angostura. Not the reverse: Angostura is what most recipes actually specify.
Lighter and unpeated. It works where the recipe wanted a blend, which is most of the Savoy.
